literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quietly rich day in the literary world, with a novel set among film sets, a few pieces on language and voice, and some lovely stories about the people who keep reading alive.

Let me begin with fiction that reaches into art and history. Literary Hub carries a conversation with Olivia Laing about her new novel, The Silver Book. It is set in the world of nineteen-seventies Italian cinema, and it concerns art, queer love and illusion, which feels like a natural home for a writer whose prose is so often described as spellbinding. If you enjoy novels that borrow the eye of a painter or a film-maker, this interview may well tempt you.

The Guardian, meanwhile, reviews Two Women, the second novel by Jacqueline Rose. It is a fictional biography that alternates between two figures: the author's sister, the philosopher Gillian Rose, and Edith Stein, another philosopher. The reviewer describes it as a memorial to Gillian, and it weaves together biography, memoir and philosophy. It sounds like the kind of book that teaches you a life of thought through the pull of a story, rather than through a lecture.

Now to prizes and shortlists. ScottishNews.com reports that Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won the Scottish Book of the Year and made history with the award. It's a heartening result for a novelist whose Glasgow setting and vivid characters have won so many admirers. And The Independent has a critic who has read all six novels on the Booker Prize shortlist and names the one to pick up. I don't have the title to hand, but if you'd like to read along before the winner is announced, it's a handy guide to where to start.

On to language itself, which is where today's most lyrical writing seems to be. Literary Hub publishes a reflection on what it means to be a Basque writer. It centres on the beauty of the language and on the grief of hearing it slowly die out. It is a lovely piece for anyone who loves the sound of words, and it may be worth a thought for your students, too, about what a language carries with it.

Literary Hub also offers a short story called Hello Daughter. Its central character, Lori, hasn't heard from her daughter Freddie in about a week, and she isn't sure of her current address. Their weekly exchange is simply "hi", followed by the reply, "I'm still not dead." That small, dry line carries a quietly sharp emotional charge. It's the sort of compact piece that could open up a good discussion about voice and subtext.

In the same spirit, there is a personal essay on how online fandom made a writer. She describes herself as an only child who preferred fictional worlds, and she traces how she found her way from reading and imagining to writing, through fandom communities. It's a nice reminder that the road into authorship isn't always the one we expect, and teenagers may well recognise themselves in it.

Finally, a cluster of stories about libraries, reading and the people who champion them. Literary Hub's weekly history piece looks back to seventeen thirty-one, when Benjamin Franklin conceived the idea of a lending library in colonial America. Books were rare and costly then, and the piece marks the moment the first ten members joined. It's a short, pleasing slice of reading history.

From the present day comes a heartening story from Santa Cruz, California. On Tuesday the sixth of October, during Banned Books Week, three high school seniors organised a sold-out benefit screening of the twenty twenty-five documentary The Librarians. It's good to see young people taking up the cause of libraries and reading so energetically.

The Guardian, for its part, talks to Liz Pichon as her Tom Gates series turns fifteen. She speaks about overcoming dyslexia to become a bestselling children's author, and about the secrets behind the series, summed up in the headline phrase "No tech, no texts, just childhood." It's warm and personal, though aimed at younger readers than the ones you teach. Still, the story of dyslexia and persistence is one that might be worth passing on.

And one more for the history-through-reading shelf: Literary Hub has a list of seventeen books on Native American culture to read this November, drawn from university presses, which publish much of the field's scholarship. The excerpt I have is cut short, so I can't tell you the full range of the list, but it may be a good place to look for books that teach history from within the cultures they describe.

So there's a good spread today, from film sets and philosophers to a vanishing language and a very short, very sharp conversation between a mother and daughter. I hope something here finds its way onto your reading pile, perhaps with a cup of something warm and a view of Belledonne.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna, and welcome to your literature briefing for this Monday, with a morning's worth of stories about illusion, language, prizes, and the quiet places where readers are made.

Let me begin with the writing that seems most likely to stay with you, starting with Olivia Laing. Literary Hub has published a conversation with her about her new novel, The Silver Book. It is set in the world of 1970s Italian cinema, and she talks about it as a book concerned with art, queer love and illusion. I'd say that combination is made for you. You enjoy stories you can step into without already knowing the culture, and a film world of that period is exactly the sort of place where the glamour and the artifice are part of the subject. Illusion is a theme that works on two levels, in the lives of the characters and in the way a novel casts its own spell. The piece describes her prose as spellbinding, and since you respond so strongly to beautiful language, it may be worth reading the interview first and then seeing whether the opening pages live up to what she says about them. It is also a book that sits close to painting and image-making, which is a link you tend to enjoy following.

Staying with fiction that carries history and thought, The Guardian has a review of Two Women, the second novel by Jacqueline Rose. It is a fictional biography built on alternating chapters. In one strand is the author's sister, Gillian Rose, and in the other the philosopher Edith Stein. The reviewer describes it as a memorial to Gillian, and as a weaving together of biography, memoir and philosophy. I find the structure appealing. Two lives set side by side, never quite meeting on the page, but each lighting the other. It is the kind of book that teaches thinking through a person rather than through an argument, which is close to what you value in novels that teach history better than history essays do. The grief behind it, a sister remembered through fiction, adds a layer of feeling to what might otherwise be a very intellectual project. If you read only the review, you will still come away with a sense of how unusual the form is.

And there is a third piece in this lyrical vein, a reflection in Literary Hub titled What It Means To Be a Basque Writer. It centres on language: its beauty, and the grief of hearing a language die out. I would call it the most musical item of the morning, because it is about the sound and survival of words, not just their meaning. For someone who teaches English to young people who move between languages, as your pupils at the lycée surely do, there is something moving in a writer thinking about what is lost when a tongue falls silent. It might even make a thoughtful starting point for a conversation with an older class about what it means to write in one language rather than another, and what a language carries that translation cannot.

Now to prizes, which are in the air this week. In Scotland, Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won the Scottish Book of the Year and, according to ScottishNews.com, made history with the award. The report doesn't spell out the detail of what makes it historic in the material I have, so I won't guess, but it is clearly a landmark moment. It is a heartening result for a novelist whose strength lies in his characters and his Glasgow setting. Shuggie Bain is one of those books where the place and the people seem inseparable, and the voice sits so close to its characters that you feel you are standing in the room with them. If you have already read it, this is a happy reminder. If you have not, it is a good moment to consider it, especially for older pupils who enjoy fiction with a distinct sense of place and speech.

Then there is the Booker Prize. The Independent's critic has read all six shortlisted novels and names the one to pick up. I don't have the title from my notes, I'm afraid, so that is something you will have to discover by reading the piece itself. But the idea is useful. If you like to read before a winner is announced, so that you have your own opinion rather than borrowing one, a single critic's recommendation from the six can be a sensible way into the shortlist. You might find that you agree, or, just as pleasingly, that you don't.

Let me turn now to something quite different, and rather touching: stories about how people become readers and writers. Literary Hub has a personal essay called How Online Fandom Made Me a Writer. The writer describes herself as an only child who preferred fictional worlds to the real one, and who found her way into writing through online fandom. I like the honesty of that route. People often assume that writers are formed by the classics, and yet so many begin by inhabiting someone else's invented world and then wanting to add to it. It is a reflection on reading, imagination and becoming an author, and it could be a gentle way into a conversation with seconde pupils, many of whom are probably doing something very similar online without thinking of it as writing at all. It might help to show them that borrowed worlds can be a real apprenticeship in storytelling.

A similar thread runs through The Guardian's interview with Liz Pichon, whose Tom Gates series turns fifteen this year. She talks about overcoming dyslexia to become a bestselling children's author, and the piece is warm and personal. The headline quotes her on the secrets behind the series: no tech, no texts, just childhood. It is aimed at a younger readership than the one you teach, but it holds something that matters to any teacher of literature. Here is a writer for whom reading and writing were once difficult, and who went on to sell millions of books to children. For a pupil who struggles with the page, that is a quietly encouraging story, and one worth keeping in your pocket.

On the fiction side, Literary Hub has also published a short story called Hello Daughter. It is about a woman named Lori, who has not heard from her daughter Freddie in about a week, and who is not sure of her current address. Their weekly exchange is very simple. Lori writes "hi", and Freddie replies, "I'm still not dead." That small, sharp reply carries a great deal. It is funny and bleak at once, and it shows how much feeling can be packed into very few words. I think it would repay a close reading, since so much of the story seems to live in what is not said. As an example of economy and subtext, a pair of lines like that could be a lovely thing to put in front of a première class and ask them what the relationship between the two women actually is.

Finally, a group of pieces about libraries, reading and the history of books, which feel gathered together rather naturally this morning.

Literary Hub's weekly literary history column looks back to Benjamin Franklin's idea, in seventeen thirty-one, for a lending library in colonial America. This was a time when books were rare and costly, and the notion of pooling resources so that members could borrow rather than buy was a small revolution in how people could read. The piece is described as a short and pleasing slice of reading history, and the headline tells us that America's first lending library gets its first ten members. There is something lovely about that number. Ten people, one shared shelf, and the start of something that would grow far beyond them.

And that story has a very modern echo. Also in Literary Hub, there is a report from Santa Cruz, California, where, on Tuesday the sixth of October, during Banned Books Week, three high school seniors organised a sold-out benefit screening of the twenty twenty-five documentary The Librarians. The audience watched it alongside librarians. I find it heartening that young people were the ones organising, and that the event sold out. It suggests that the defence of libraries and of reading freely is something teenagers are willing to take on themselves, rather than waiting to be told. It sits well beside the Franklin piece, with one story at the beginning of the lending library and the other showing people still working to protect it nearly three hundred years later.

Last, there is a Literary Hub list of seventeen books about Native American culture to read this November, drawn from university presses, which publish much of the scholarship in this field. I should be honest that the excerpt I have is cut short, so I can't tell you exactly what the list covers or how it is organised. But the premise is a good one, and suits a reader who likes books that teach history. University press titles can be less visible than the big trade releases, so a list gathered from them may point you towards things you would not otherwise stumble upon. It may be worth a look, if only to see what is on offer.

So that is the morning: a novel of cinematic illusion, a sister remembered through philosophy, a language held in grief, a Glasgow novelist honoured, six Booker novels narrowed to one recommendation, a girl who writes only "I'm still not dead", and three teenagers filling a room to defend the library that Franklin's ten members began.

Enjoy your coffee and whichever of these pages calls to you first.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the ninth of November, and the news from the art world today has a pleasantly literary slant, with a good deal happening close to home at the Musée de Grenoble.

Let me start there, since the museum has a busy few weeks ahead. Today at half past two, the Amis du musée are screening and discussing Caroline Champetier's 2012 film about Berthe Morisot. It's a chance to see how a filmmaker approaches a painter's life and work, and if your Monday allows it, it's a lovely way to spend an afternoon.

The museum is also in the middle of its exhibition devoted to the American sculptor Anne Truitt, called "Libérer la couleur". There was a guided tour of it yesterday afternoon, which you've just missed, but what I like is how the museum is building a programme around her. On the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the actor Anne Castillo will perform readings from Truitt's journal, under the title "Au fil des jours", directed by Mathieu Barché. Truitt was a sculptor, but here it's her own written voice that takes the stage, which seems made for you: an artist's private prose, read aloud, in front of the work.

Then on Thursday at half past twelve there's a lunchtime concert, "Couleurs d'automne", as part of the museum's music series. It's a short listening break, well suited to a midday visit. And from Saturday, the fourteenth, the museum opens an exhibition on Edmund Kesting, presented as painter, photographer and advertising artist. I find that mix intriguing, because it sets fine art beside commercial image-making, and it's not an angle one often meets.

Beyond the museum, the local press has a few pointers, though I should be honest that some of them are thin on detail. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on an exhibition in Saint-Martin-d'Hères that retraces forty years of painting and spiritual searching. The theme sounds personal and contemplative, but the text gives no dates, so it would be worth checking before you set out. The same paper has a guide to the must-see events of the Mois de la photo in Grenoble, and another piece on an exhibition at the Hang'Art in Grenoble, which its curators built on instinct rather than around a fixed theme. In both cases I only have the headlines, so I can't tell you which photographers or artists are involved, but they're worth keeping an eye on. There's also a short piece from l'Essentiel asking what history lies behind the walls of the Magasin-CNAC, one of the city's key contemporary art venues. And a contemporary art biennale called "Rêves en Tête" is advertised by jds.fr, featuring the sculptor eOle and invited artists, though the location isn't stated, so I can't say whether it's within reach of Les Adrets.

Now, to the stories where painting and writing meet, which I think you'll enjoy most.

The Guardian has a moving piece by Cordelia Roche about her father, the poet Paul Roche, and his thirty-year relationship with the Bloomsbury painter Duncan Grant. He was Grant's friend and muse, she says, but never his lover. The title comes from a line she remembers: "My father loved Duncan more than he loved us". It's a personal account of growing up in a family raised in the image of the Bloomsbury world, and it's tied to a major exhibition of Grant's work. It reads almost like a memoir, with a strong narrator, and might make a good starting point for a conversation with older students about how the lives of artists and writers intertwine.

Also in The Guardian, there's the story of Louise Cansot, the model behind what became known as "the girl of 100 portraits". She was murdered in Paris in 1949, and the police forgot about her. Her story has inspired two books, one of them a Goncourt-winning novel, and a historical research project too. It's a story that links painting, fiction and the patient work of recovery, which is precisely the kind of history that a novel can make felt, in a way an essay seldom can.

From Beaux Arts Magazine comes a quick profile of Séraphine Louis, known as Séraphine de Senlis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She was a pioneer of naïve art, self-taught, and her paintings are exuberant. It's only a two-minute read, but she is such a vivid character that the profile is a pleasure, and she would sit nicely beside the other figures I've mentioned.

One more from The Guardian, though a harder one. It's a review of "A Fox Under a Pink Moon", a film assembled from five years of smartphone footage of Soraya Akhlaghi, who fled Iran as a teenager and was filmed through her precarious new life. The reviewer calls it a boldly imaginative self-portrait, and it is as much about her voice as a narrator as about her circumstances. It sounds like a remarkable character study, but a harrowing one, so perhaps one for a day when you're feeling steady.

So, in short, an afternoon with Morisot today, a lunchtime concert on Thursday, Kesting from Saturday, and Anne Truitt's own words in December.

Have a lovely day, Yamuna, and may the autumn light be kind in the valley.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the ninth of November, and the last couple of days have brought a pleasant mix of things to do close to home, and some stories about painters and the writers who loved them.

Let me begin in Grenoble, at the Musée de Grenoble, which has quite a lot going on this week and beyond.

The nearest thing is this afternoon. At half past two, the Amis du musée are hosting a talk that screens and discusses Caroline Champetier's 2012 film on Berthe Morisot. It's an interesting idea: a filmmaker, and a cinematographer by trade, turning her eye on a painter who spent her career thinking about light, surface and the fleeting moment. A film about a painter is always a translation of one medium into another, and a talk afterwards is the right place to ask how well it's done. If you can slip away this afternoon, it sounds like a rewarding hour.

On Thursday, the twelfth, at half past twelve, there's a lunchtime concert called Couleurs d'automne, part of the Musée en musique series. It's a short listening break in the middle of the day, and the title suits the season. The leaves in the Grésivaudan must be turning properly by now, and there is something nice about hearing music with autumn in its name while looking at colour on the walls. I don't have the programme or the performers, but the format, a brief concert at midday, is made for fitting into a working day.

Then on Saturday, the fourteenth, a new exhibition opens at the museum, devoted to Edmund Kesting. The billing describes him as painter, photographer and advertising artist, and I rather like that combination. We tend to separate fine art from commercial image-making, as though they lived in different houses, and here is an artist who moved between them. Seeing how a painter's eye shapes an advertisement, or how a photographer's discipline feeds a canvas, could make for a thoughtful visit. It might also give you something to talk about with your première students when you discuss how images persuade us, which is, after all, not far from how a writer persuades with words.

Alongside that, the museum's exhibition on Anne Truitt, called Libérer la couleur, is still on. There was a guided tour yesterday afternoon, Sunday, at half past two, so that one has just passed, but the exhibition itself continues, and you can go and look at your own pace. What I find most appealing is what's coming in December. On the twelfth and thirteenth, the actor Anne Castillo will perform readings from Truitt's journal, under the title Au fil des jours, directed by Mathieu Barché. Truitt was a sculptor, someone who worked in colour and form, and here you will hear her in her own written voice. For a lover of fiction, narrators and beautiful prose, there's something special about an artist's journal read aloud. A journal is a narrator without a plot, someone simply watching her days go by and setting them down. It would be worth putting those December dates in the diary now, and perhaps visiting the exhibition beforehand so the words arrive already attached to the work.

Now a little further into the local scene, where I have several leads but they're thin on detail, so I'll be honest about what I know.

In Saint-Martin-d'Hères, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on an exhibition that retraces forty years of painting and spiritual searching. The theme is personal and contemplative, a lifetime's work seen as a kind of inner journey. The text I have doesn't give dates or the venue, so you would need to check before making the trip, but it's close to Grenoble and sounds like the sort of small, sincere show that can stay with you.

Le Dauphiné Libéré also has a guide to the must-see events of the Mois de la photo in Grenoble. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you which exhibitions they single out, but it does tell us that the photography month is under way in the city, and it would be worth looking up that guide. Given your taste for local shows, there may be something among those events that sits well with the Kesting exhibition, since he was a photographer too.

And at the Hang'Art in Grenoble, there is an exhibition the curators say they built on instinct rather than around a fixed theme. Again I only have the headline, so I can't name the artists or works. But I like the idea. A show assembled by instinct is a bit like a good anthology: the connections emerge from the feeling of the pieces rather than from a thesis, and you're invited to find your own thread.

There's also a short piece from l'Essentiel asking what history lies behind the walls of the Magasin-CNAC in Grenoble. It is one of the city's key contemporary art venues, and the question of its building and its past is a nice one. A place where art is shown has its own story, layered under the exhibitions, and it's the sort of local history that makes a familiar building look different the next time you walk past it. I don't have the answer the article gives, only the question, but it may well be worth a read.

One more item, further afield, and I can say little about it: a contemporary art biennale called Rêves en Tête, featuring the sculptor eOle and invited artists. The source is jds.fr, and the location isn't stated, so I'll simply leave it as a name to keep in mind. It's a lovely title, though, a dream in the head.

Now to the stories behind the art, which I think you'll enjoy most, because they are really about people.

The Guardian has a personal piece by Cordelia Roche about her father, the poet Paul Roche, and his thirty-year bond with the Bloomsbury painter Duncan Grant. She recalls that Grant was a friend and a muse to her father, but never a lover, and the headline carries the sharp line, "My father loved Duncan more than he loved us." That's a remarkable sentence to build a family memoir around. The piece is tied to a major exhibition of Grant's work, and it takes us into the Bloomsbury world, where painting and writing were so closely intertwined. Think of it as a narrator's voice, a daughter looking back at a household shaped by a devotion that sat just outside the ordinary categories, and at a family raised, in the words of the headline, in the image of that circle. If you ever teach anything from Bloomsbury, this is the kind of human detail that makes the period come alive for students: not only the manifestos and the canvases, but the long, complicated loyalties underneath.

The second Guardian piece is, I think, the one that fits you best. It's about Louise Cansot, the model behind what became known as "the girl of 100 portraits". She was murdered in Paris in 1949, and her death was then forgotten by the police. The story has inspired two books, and the article draws together painting, a Goncourt-winning novel and a historical research project. It's a fine example of what you like most: fiction and research combining to recover a history that official records let slip. A woman who was painted a hundred times, and yet whose own story went unattended, is a haunting image, and it raises the question that so many novels ask: who gets looked at, and who gets remembered? The Goncourt connection means that at least one of those books has already found a wide readership in France, and the piece sets it alongside the research that stands behind it. If you've time for only one article from today, I'd suggest this.

Staying with strong lives, Beaux Arts Magazine offers a quick two-minute profile of Séraphine Louis, known as Séraphine de Senlis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. She is described as a pioneer of naïve art, and the piece celebrates her exuberant paintings. Self-taught artists make wonderful characters, because their work arrives without the usual apparatus of training or fashion, and the profile is brief enough to read in a spare moment. It might also make a nice small thing to share with a class. A short, vivid biography of someone who painted outside every rule is a good way into conversations about what counts as art and who decides.

Last, a film, though not the usual sort of film news. The Guardian reviews A Fox Under a Pink Moon, assembled from five years of smartphone footage by Soraya Akhlaghi, who fled Iran as a teenager. She was filmed through her precarious new life, and the reviewer calls it a boldly imaginative self-portrait. What stands out for you, I think, is the narrator's own voice. A story told by the person living it, in fragments captured on a phone, is close to a first-person novel in how it works, with the self shaping the account as it goes. I should warn you that the review describes it as harrowing, so it's one to approach when you feel ready for it, but it sounds like a strong and unusual character study.

So, to sum up the practical points: this afternoon, the Morisot film talk at half past two; Thursday at half past twelve, the autumn concert; Saturday, the Kesting exhibition opens; the Truitt exhibition carries on, with her journal read aloud on the twelfth and thirteenth of December. In between, the Mois de la photo, the Hang'Art and the Saint-Martin-d'Hères show are all worth a look once you've checked the details.

That's your art briefing, Yamuna, and I hope something in it takes you out into the autumn light today.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for the BFI, with no official texts or reforms, but a pleasant scattering of pieces touching works on your programme, and most of them are only headlines, so I'll be honest about how much each one tells us.

Let's begin with the session twenty twenty-seven Shakespeare, since there are three items here. First, a short essay from MiscelAna marking four hundred and ten years since Shakespeare's death and asking why he still matters. It's brief, but that is rather the point: it could work as a gentle opening for seconde or première, a way into Twelfth Night or Hamlet before anyone has opened the text. You might even ask pupils to write their own answer to the question first, and then compare it with the essay's.

Second, an article from a site called 白鲸出海 on the sentry exchange in Hamlet, the line "Stand and unfold yourself", and how it may echo the royal court. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what argument it makes. But the idea is a lovely one for close reading: a play that begins with a challenge to identity, someone demanding that another person reveal who they are. It's a neat way to set up a theme that runs through the whole play, and the article may be worth a quick look before you decide whether to use it.

Third, the University of Auckland has announced the return of its summer Shakespeare, a comedy double bill. It's a very long way from Les Adrets, and I don't have details of which plays are involved. Still, it's a small reminder that Shakespearean comedy is being staged joyfully on the other side of the world, which might be a nice aside for a Twelfth Night class, particularly when pupils assume Shakespeare belongs to a very particular corner of England.

Staying with the stage, Fairy Powered Productions has published a review of its production of Great Expectations. Dickens is on the twenty twenty-seven list, so it's of obvious interest. The text is only the title, so I can't say what the production looked like or whether the review is favourable. If you're looking for a staging to discuss with première, it might be worth finding out more, particularly to ask how a theatre company handles Pip as narrator, since that voice is so much of what makes the novel.

Now to the oral themes. Maya Angelou appears twice. Vocal has a tribute titled "Celebrating Maya Angelou", though only the headline came through, so the content is unclear. And The List has a Quote of the Day from her, beginning "When I was younger, I thought my grandmother was…", and then the excerpt cuts off. It's too short to be a proper resource, but as a starter it has some charm. You could read that unfinished sentence aloud and ask pupils how they would complete it, then compare with how Angelou's prose handles memory and family in I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. It's the sort of thing that suits your love of voice and narrator.

Arab News, in its "What We Are Reading Today" column, has a piece on George Orwell's enduring argument for protecting life's simple pleasures. The text is thin, but I find the angle appealing. Orwell is usually taught through 1984 and its darkness, so a reflective discussion on what he thought was worth defending, and why, might offer a quieter way into the same book. It could make an interesting counterweight in an oral preparation session on resistance and control.

And Creative Boom features the Balbusso Twins on returning to The Handmaid's Tale. Again, only the headline, so I can't confirm what they say or which images they've made. Still, given your interest in how paintings and illustration meet written works, it may be worth a look. Visual interpretations of Atwood's novel can be a good way to get pupils talking about how a text creates its images, and whether an illustrator can capture a narrator's restricted point of view.

That leaves a handful of wider reading pieces. The Wall Street Journal has a piece on the reading list for what it calls the hottest class at Harvard. It's headline only, but it might give you a sense of how a university frames its literature teaching, and perhaps a few ideas to borrow, or argue with, for your own classes. Literary Hub asks what the best literary TV adaptation of all time is. I don't have the answer, but the question itself is a good classroom provocation, especially with Great Expectations or Emma in mind: what does a screen adaptation gain, and what does it lose? Vocal also has a list of seven great books with endings you'll never forget. It's a light read, but endings are a rich topic, and you could ask pupils to compare how Hamlet, Great Expectations and Never Let Me Go leave their audiences.

Finally, something a little different. The Independent has an interview with the actor Greg Wise, whose headline says that being there at the end of someone's life is an exquisite privilege. I only have that line, so the rest of the conversation is unknown to me. It isn't connected to the programme, but it sounds like a humane piece from an artist, and the sort you might read with a cup of tea rather than a red pen.

So, a gentle day: plenty of prompts, very little that's firm, and a good excuse to read the full articles when you have a spare moment. Have a lovely Monday.

The second item is more specific. An article from 白鲸出海 looks at the sentry exchange in Hamlet, "Stand and unfold yourself", and how it may echo the royal court. I only have the headline, so I can't say how the argument runs. But the line itself is a lovely small thing to teach. It comes at the very start of the play, in the dark, with nervous men on watch, and it is an order to reveal oneself. For a play so concerned with disguise, performance and what lies beneath the surface, that is a rich place to begin. A close reading of just those opening moments, read aloud in class and then discussed, could set up the themes of the whole play. Whether the article's link to the royals holds up, I can't say, but the headline offers a way into a conversation about how a play's first lines can quietly announce its preoccupations.

The third Shakespeare item is from the University of Auckland, which announces the return of a summer Shakespeare comedy double bill. It is a long way from Grenoble, and I have no details of which plays are involved. Still, it is a pleasant reminder that Shakespeare's comedies are being staged by students on the other side of the world this season. For Twelfth Night, it could serve as a small point of comparison: pupils might enjoy knowing that young people elsewhere are performing these plays for the pleasure of it, and it may nudge you to think about having your own class perform a scene.

Now to the staging and adaptation questions. Fairy Powered Productions has a review of a production of Great Expectations. Dickens is on the 2027 session, and a review of a staging could be useful if it turns out to be one your pupils might see or watch in some form. But the text I have is only the title, so I can't tell you anything about the production itself, its style, or whether the reviewer liked it. If you are looking for ideas, a good exercise with any stage version of the novel is to ask what has to be cut, and what a theatre does with a narrator as strong as Pip. You love a memorable narrator, and Pip is one who is constantly judging his younger self. How a stage production handles that doubled voice is a genuinely interesting classroom question.

Related to that, Literary Hub asks what the best literary television adaptation of all time might be. Again I only have the question, not the answer, so I can't tell you which titles it considers. But the question itself is a good prompt for older pupils. You could ask them to defend their own choice, and to say what makes an adaptation faithful: the plot, the tone, the language, or the feeling of reading the book. For terminale, that could be a useful way of getting students to think about what is lost and gained when a novel changes medium.

Turning to the oral themes list, there are two Maya Angelou items. The Vocal website has a tribute titled "Celebrating Maya Angelou", and The List has a quote of the day from her, which begins "When I was younger, I thought my grandmother was…" and is cut off in what I have. I can't say how the sentence finishes, so I won't guess. But it is a reminder that I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is, among other things, a book about a child's view of the adults around her, and the grandmother is a central figure in it. A short excerpt of Angelou's prose can be a fine thing to read aloud at the start of a lesson, since her sentences have a musical, spoken quality that suits the voice. If you can find the complete quote, it might make a good two-minute opening for an oral preparation session, with pupils asked to say what the voice of the narrator is doing, and how a child's view differs from an adult's.

Also on the oral list, Arab News has a reading column on George Orwell's argument for protecting life's simple pleasures. The text is thin, but it is a gentler angle on an author usually taught through 1984's bleakness. It might prompt a reflective discussion: if a totalitarian state is one that tries to control even private pleasure and private thought, what does it mean to defend simple pleasures? That would link naturally to 1984 without requiring any extra reading. I wouldn't claim more for the column than that, but the idea is a good one to take into a classroom.

On the same list, Creative Boom has a piece on the Balbusso Twins returning to The Handmaid's Tale. The headline is all I have, so I can't confirm what their work is. Creative Boom is a publication about creative work, so I would guess it is about visual interpretation of Atwood's novel, but please treat that as a guess. If it does turn out to be an artist's response, it would suit your interest in the links between painting and writing. Atwood's novel is full of strong images, the red cloaks and white bonnets above all, and asking pupils how an artist would depict Gilead, and what they would choose to leave out, is a lively way into the book's visual and symbolic language.

Finally, three pieces that don't belong to the programme but may be of interest. The Wall Street Journal has a piece on the reading list for what it calls the hottest class at Harvard. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what is on the list. Still, it could be interesting to see how a university frames a popular literature course, and whether the choices are surprising. Vocal has a list of seven great books with endings you will never forget, again headline only, but it is a nice prompt for a lesson on closure: what makes an ending feel inevitable, and what makes it feel earned. You could set pupils the task of writing the last paragraph of a novel they know well. And The Independent has an interview with the actor Greg Wise, in which he calls being present at the end of someone's life an exquisite privilege. I only have that headline, so I can't tell you more, but it sounds like a thoughtful, humane conversation with an artist.

That is the whole of it. Mostly these are small prompts rather than news, but Hamlet's sentries and Pip's voice are both good places to start the week. Have a lovely day, Yamuna.

Tomorrow, Tuesday the tenth of November, at seven in the evening, there's an evening at the Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot devoted to the photographer Vivian Maier, under the title "Tout entière". Again there's no further detail, but a title about light might well speak to someone who loves painting.

Two other things deserve a mention for the MC2 and Grenoble's theatres. Throughout November, the MC2 is offering free cultural activities for people with disabilities, which is a lovely thing to see in a major venue's programme. And jds.fr reports on a guided visit behind the scenes at the Grand Théâtre de Grenoble. The text doesn't give a date, so you'd need to check, but for someone who loves theatre and stories, seeing how a stage actually works is a real treat.

Hervé Frumy's exhibition "Les Yeux Ouverts" at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage closed yesterday, after opening at the end of September. So, the week begins with Vivian Maier and ends with fire in the foothills, and I hope there's a candle-lit evening or two in between. Have a lovely Monday, Yamuna.
around.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the ninth of November, and the next few weeks around you are rather good for stories, music and images, with a few things just behind us and a handsome cluster of December evenings to plan for.

Let me begin with the nearest dates, because two of them fall tomorrow, Tuesday the tenth of November, and they pull in slightly different directions.

The first is at Espace Aragon in Villard-Bonnot, at seven in the evening. It's part of a series called "One evening, one artist", and this time the artist is the photographer Vivian Maier. The evening is titled "Tout entière", which one might translate as "Whole", or "In her entirety". I mention it with you in mind, because Maier's work sits so well beside your interest in how images and written narrative speak to each other. A photograph can be read almost like a very short story, with a narrator you never see and a character caught mid-sentence. If you've ever thought of bringing a photograph into a lesson on voice or point of view, an evening like this might hand you a few ideas. It's in Villard-Bonnot, so quite close to home, down in the Grésivaudan.

The second event on Tuesday is in Eybens, and it's a ciné-concert of a film called "Mobile Homes". A ciné-concert is a film shown while the music is performed live, so the soundtrack is not a recording but something happening in the room, beside you, in real time. Le Dauphiné Libéré flags it as taking place this Tuesday. The details in the article are slim, so I can't tell you more about the musicians or the evening's length. But for someone who loves both music and storytelling, the form itself is the attraction. Eybens is on the far side of Grenoble from you, so it's a little more of a journey than Villard-Bonnot, and of course you can't be in both places at once. It's rather a pleasant dilemma to have on a Tuesday in November.

Still in the same week, on Thursday the twelfth of November at eight in the evening, there's a talk about the lynx in the Chartreuse massif. It takes place at the Pôle Artistique et Culturel in Le Touvet. This is a nature evening rather than a literary one, but it concerns the mountains on your doorstep, across the valley from Belledonne. It's an elusive animal, and a talk about it has a certain quiet appeal. I wouldn't presume to say what will be covered, as the listing gives no further detail. But if you like knowing who shares the hillsides with you, it's a good reason to drive down to Le Touvet on a dark November evening.

Then a little further ahead, on Sunday the fifteenth of November, there's a fire show at Crêts-en-Belledonne. Le Dauphiné Libéré announces it, though the piece I have is really only the headline, so I can't tell you the time, the company, or whether it's a performance in the street or somewhere indoors. What I can say is that it's a village event in the foothills of your own massif, and fire in mid-November, with the evenings so early and so cold, has something rather fitting about it. It's worth keeping the date free and looking for the details nearer the time.

Now, a few things that have just slipped by, which I mention so you don't go chasing them. Yesterday, Sunday the eighth, was the last day of Hervé Frumy's exhibition "Les Yeux Ouverts", at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage. It had been running since the twenty-sixth of September, so if you managed to see it, wonderful, and if not, that's one for the notebook of things to catch next time. The same day there was an autumn producers' market at the salle des fêtes in Saint-Vincent-de-Mercuze, from ten in the morning until six in the evening, and a performance called "Poucette" at Le Coléo in Pontcharra. I have no description of that piece, so I can't tell you what it was like. All three are now past, but they show how lively the valley is at this time of year, with markets and exhibitions and theatre all within a short drive.

If you're missing the exhibitions, the good news is that two others are still open, and they'll stay open for a good while. The first is by Jean-Pierre Angei, titled "Il soffio del tempo", which means "the breath of time". It's in Villard-Bonnot, it opened on the seventh of November, and it runs until the sixth of January, and it's free. The listing says very little more than that, so I can't tell you whether it's paintings, drawings or something else. But the title is lovely, and it has that slightly musical quality you tend to enjoy. Since it's in Villard-Bonnot, you could happily pair it with the Maier evening tomorrow, arriving a little early to see the exhibition before the talk, if the opening hours allow. I'd check that locally before setting off.

The second is a free exhibition at Saint-Martin-d'Hères called "À la conquête de l'eau", the conquest of water, in Isère in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It started on the nineteenth of September and runs until the third of April next year, so there's no rush at all. It's a piece of local history, and I think it may appeal to the part of you that likes to learn how the past is told. Water, in this region of mountains, torrents and valleys, has shaped so much, and an exhibition about how people set about taming and using it should have plenty of human stories inside it. It's the sort of thing that could sit nicely alongside a novel set in a landscape where the weather and the land are practically characters.

Now to the heart of the matter, I think, which is December at the MC2 in Grenoble. Four things are clustered into a few days, and it would be a shame to miss the chance to plan them together.

The one I'd put first for you is "Ivanov", by Anton Chekhov, staged by Jean-François Sivadier. It runs from the second to the fourth of December. A major Russian play, in a production close to home, is a rare thing, and for a teacher of literature it has obvious pleasures. Chekhov is a master of the character who can't quite say what he means, whose life drifts on the page in small, aching increments. I'd rather not say more about this particular production than the listing allows, as I only know the director and the dates. But if you've ever wanted to see how a stage handles that kind of quiet, interior drama, this is the opportunity. It would also give you something to talk about with your students, even if they have never opened a Russian play.

The very next evening, Thursday the third of December, and again on Friday the fourth, the MC2 has "Mussum", a dance piece by Souhail Marchiche and Mehdi Meghari of the company Dyptik. The text I have gives no further detail, so I can't describe the choreography or the mood of it. But as someone who enjoys dance, and especially watching how movement can tell a story without a single word, you may find it worth the evening. Dyptik is a contemporary dance company, so I'd expect something quite different from the classical repertoire, but I shouldn't say more than I know.

On that same Friday the fourth of December, the MC2 also hosts the Orchestre national de Lyon, playing Webern, Britten and Brahms. The soloist is the violinist Vilde Frang, and the conductor is Nikolaj Szeps-Znaider. It's a strong classical programme, and the three names make an interesting journey, from the very compressed and delicate to the full, warm Romantic sound at the end. I'll leave it to you to decide whether you want to do the Brahms-and-Britten evening or the dance, since both fall on the Friday. The Thursday gives you a clean choice for dance, and the Wednesday, if the Ivanov performances are spread across the three days, may suit the theatre. I'd look at the exact times on the MC2 listings to see how the days fit together.

Then, on Sunday the sixth of December, again at the MC2, there's a Sunday concert by the Ensemble Les Illuminations, called "Jouer la lumière", or "Playing the light". The text gives no details of the programme, so I can't say what music will be played. But the title alone has a pleasing resonance with painting, and with the long tradition of writers and artists who have tried to catch light, whether in oils or in words. A Sunday concert is also a gentle way to close a week in which, if you've said yes to everything, you will have been out rather a lot.

Two more items are worth knowing about at the MC2 and the Grand Théâtre. The first is an article in jds.fr about a guided visit behind the scenes at the Grand Théâtre de Grenoble. The text doesn't give a date, so I can't tell you when it's happening, but it describes a rare look at how a stage works: the machinery, the spaces the audience never sees. For a reader who loves theatre and stories, that backstage view has its own fascination, and it might be worth contacting the theatre to find out when the next visit is. It could even make a useful outing for a class, though I wouldn't promise that without knowing the details.

The second is from mesinfos, and it concerns free cultural activities for people with disabilities, which are taking place at the MC2 throughout November. I don't have the individual activities or times, but it's good to see a major cultural venue making room for everyone, and it's a warm note to include on a grey November morning.

So, to gather it together: tomorrow offers Vivian Maier in Villard-Bonnot or a ciné-concert in Eybens, Thursday brings the lynx at Le Touvet, and the fifteenth has fire in the foothills at Crêts-en-Belledonne. Two exhibitions are open for weeks to come, and early December at the MC2 is rich with Chekhov, dance, Brahms and light.

Whichever evening you choose, I hope it's a good one, and that the walk back to the car is crisp and starlit.

Good morning, Yamuna. Here is a gentle tour of France over the last two days, beginning with something that touches your working week and moving on to books, a little good news, and a few small pleasures.

First, schools. The Local France reports that student and teacher groups have called a strike for tomorrow, Tuesday the tenth of November, with demonstrations planned, including a major one expected in Paris. They are pressing the government for more spending on education, and this follows several weeks of school closures and protests. HugoDécrypte also flagged the call, which covers both schools and higher education, though the video gives few details. If you are at the lycée tomorrow, it is worth checking how things stand with your colleagues this evening.

Meanwhile, franceinfo says the education minister, Edouard Geffray, has again refused to move the dates of the baccalauréat, despite the hours lost in blockaded lycées. He made the point in an interview with Le Parisien, where he also said he wants greater transparency about Parcoursup. And this afternoon, the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, is due to meet representatives of lycéens and students, so there may be news by tonight.

Now to books, which I suspect is where you will want to linger. The Local France reports that the winner of this year's Prix Goncourt has defended his use of artificial intelligence in his much-praised novel. He describes it as playful, ironic and very limited, so not a machine writing the book, but something closer to a wink inside it. It is the sort of thing your première pupils might enjoy arguing about: what we expect an author to do, and what counts as the author's voice.

Staying with the prizes, franceinfo has a thoughtful piece asking why the main French literary prizes, the Goncourt among them, have all gone to men this season, after several years in which women won. The article looks at the circumstances of this particular year, but also at wider causes, and one person in it says it feels like a step backwards. It is a good reminder of how much a single season's list can tell us, and how little.

There is a link with history and fiction too. Franceinfo reviews "À jamais les premières", a Spanish comedy about the women who pioneered football under General Franco's dictatorship. It shows how they fought for a place on the pitch, and in society more broadly. It is a film rather than a novel, but it is another case of a story teaching history with a light touch.

Two pieces this weekend concern the freedom of the press. In Paris, on Wednesday the eleventh of November, a charity football match will mark five hundred days of detention in Algeria for the French journalist Christophe Gleizes. Reporters sans frontières and the Paris city hall are organising it, to call for his release. And franceinfo looks at Russia, where Novaya Gazeta, the independent newspaper, is closing its Moscow office, having already stopped printing in 2022. The piece traces how independent journalism there was silenced or pushed into exile, and also how reporters have found new ways of working. It is a sobering read, but with a thread of stubbornness and ingenuity running through it.

On to some warmer news. HugoDécrypte has a video about "Les Vingt-cinq Heures qui courent", a charity relay that raised nearly one and a half million euros. The details are thin, but it is a heartening number for a day of running.

For daily life, there is a small piece of good news for anyone who rents. Franceinfo reports that from the twentieth of November, new measures from a rental platform will mean landlords can no longer ask tenants to tidy and clean as much as before. Tenants interviewed say they are glad of it, and one puts it nicely: you cannot do everything, after all.

The Local France also offers a practical roundup of life in France. It covers how to report bank fraud, how to manage menopause, the return of pet passports for travel between the EU and the UK, and a run of Second World War films in French cinemas. The pet passport and menopause pieces look the most useful in everyday terms.

And since the season is approaching, the same outlet has a guide to ten of the best Christmas markets in France this year, as towns begin preparing their streets and squares for the festive season. The text is brief, but it might give you ideas for a weekend outing, perhaps with a detour through a producers' market.

Finally, La Mire's round-up of French television for Saturday the seventh of November. It covers a school bus accident in the Ain, a wave of bomb hoaxes affecting flights across Europe, and reports on Chinese carmakers. It is a quick way to see how the day's stories were framed on screen.

That is all for today, Yamuna, so I hope tomorrow's strike is calm and that you find a good book and a warm drink waiting for you this evening.

He made the point in an interview with Le Parisien, where he also said he wants more transparency about Parcoursup, the platform that handles applications to higher education. There is a further development this afternoon. Franceinfo says the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, will meet representatives of lycéens and students on Monday afternoon. We don't yet know what will come of it, but it will shape how tomorrow's mobilisation looks. As a teacher, you will know the particular strain of this kind of moment: pupils who feel they have lost time, a fixed exam calendar, and a lot of uncertainty about how to make up the ground. I'll keep an eye on whether the meeting changes the tone.

Now to books, which I suspect is where you would prefer to linger. The Local France reports that the winner of this year's Prix Goncourt has defended his use of artificial intelligence in his acclaimed novel. He describes it as playful, ironic and very limited. That is a fascinating thing to hear from the author of France's most celebrated prize-winning novel, and I think it will interest you as both a reader and a teacher of fiction. The question of what it means for a narrator's voice to be partly shaped by a machine is one that could easily find its way into a classroom discussion, particularly with older pupils. The author's own framing, playful and ironic, suggests he sees it less as a shortcut and more as a literary device, a way of putting a kind of artificial voice inside the story and letting the reader notice it. I would be curious to know whether your pupils would feel that distinction matters.

Alongside that, franceinfo has an examination of something many in the literary world have noticed. The major French literary prizes this season, the Goncourt among them, have all gone to men, after several recent years in which women won. One person quoted in the piece describes the feeling of "a regression". The article looks at both the particular circumstances of this year's selections and the wider causes behind the pattern, rather than simply pointing a finger. It's a thoughtful read if you're interested in how literary reputations are made, and who gets to be seen as the voice of a season.

A little further afield, franceinfo reviews a Spanish comedy, which in French is called "À jamais les premières", about the women who pioneered football in Spain under General Franco's dictatorship. It tells how they fought for room on the pitch and, more broadly, for space in a society that did not want to give it to them. It is a film rather than a novel, but it follows a pattern you enjoy: history told through characters and a story rather than a textbook, and comedy used to carry something serious. The review suggests it manages to be funny while still showing what these women were up against.

Next, two stories about the freedom to report and to write. On Wednesday the eleventh of November, in Paris, a charity football match will mark five hundred days of detention for the French journalist Christophe Gleizes in Algeria. It is organised by Reporters sans frontières together with Paris city hall, and the aim is to call for his release. Franceinfo carries the details. It is a quiet, human way of keeping a name in the public mind, and the choice of a sporting event is a reminder that these campaigns often rely on very ordinary gestures.

The independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta is closing its Moscow office today, having already stopped printing in 2022. The article traces how Vladimir Putin's government silenced or pushed into exile much of Russia's independent press, and how journalists have since reinvented their work, finding new ways to report. The headline quotes the idea that any popular media outlet must fall under the Kremlin's control. For someone who loves the literature of the twentieth century, there are inevitable echoes of writers and editors working under pressure, and of the way words become dangerous when someone decides they are. It is a sober read, but one that tells a story of persistence as well as loss.

Let me turn now to some warmer news. HugoDécrypte has a video about the charity relay "Les 25 Heures qui courent", which has raised nearly one and a half million euros. I only have the headline and a short description, so I can't tell you much about the event itself, but it is a heartening figure, and a good reminder that a lot of people were willing to run, or sponsor someone running, for a good cause.

There is also a small piece of good news for anyone who rents. Franceinfo reports that from the twentieth of November, new measures introduced by a rental platform mean landlords will no longer be able to ask tenants to tidy and clean quite so much before leaving or during a tenancy. Among them are guidance on how to report bank fraud, a piece on managing menopause, the return of pet passports for travel between the EU and the United Kingdom, and a run of Second World War films in French cinemas. The ones that seem most immediately useful are the pet passport and menopause pieces, and if you are planning any travel with an animal, the passport news may be worth a look. The text I have is brief, so I can't tell you which towns made the list, but with the weeks of Advent approaching it may be worth a glance if you enjoy a market. I imagine a few of the producers' markets around the Grésivaudan will be thinking along the same lines.

It covers a school bus accident in the Ain, a wave of bomb hoaxes affecting flights across Europe, and reports on Chinese carmakers. It is a quick and light way of seeing how the day's stories were framed on screen, if you have a few minutes to spare with your coffee.

That's the France briefing for today, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you gently, whatever the strike brings.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news is a gentle mix of long journeys, small kindnesses, books, and a few animals who have landed on their feet.

Let me begin with the stories that are really about people finding one another. The Good News Network reports that Karl Bushby, a British former paratrooper, has finished a walk around the world. He set out from Hull in 1998, and twenty-eight years later he has come home to Hull on foot, where his mother was waiting. Apparently there were tears, and a very long-awaited hug. It has the shape of an old adventure novel, with the leaving, the wandering, and the return to the front door.

From the same source comes a quieter story with a similar arc. Thirty years ago, a Korean schoolgirl had her hanbok slashed in a racist attack, and a Japanese teenager put his coat over her shoulders. She kept that coat for three decades. Now she has found the boy who gave it to her, and the coat has been returned to him. Upworthy has a neighbourly one as well. An artist was evicted after forty years by a landlord's family who wanted to claim her hand-painted murals. A neighbour with a paint sprayer then offered her a parting gift, and the piece calls it perfect. I'll leave you to discover it, but it touches on art, place, and who a wall really belongs to. And if you would like something longer to watch, ARTE Regards has a thirty-two-minute documentary from 2021, still available until April 2030. Now to books, language, and music. ScottishNews.com reports that Douglas Stuart, author of Shuggie Bain, has won the Scottish Book of the Year and made history with the award. It is a heartening result for a writer whose Glasgow setting and fiercely drawn characters have won so many readers.

There is also a charming little piece on language from Upworthy. Stevie Nicks reportedly misheard a Southern woman's accent, and that one misheard vowel inspired one of her best-known songs. It is a small reminder of how a slip of the ear can become art. Upworthy also recalls a December 1964 performance by The Seekers, described as two minutes of musical perfection. The clip is decades old rather than new, but it may be a pleasant way to start a morning.

On to the animals. Upworthy tells of a man who raised an orphaned otter called Leya and then released her into the wild. He has filmed her swimming out to his kayak for cuddles. A wild creature choosing to come back to say hello is about as tender as these stories get.

Back in England, the Good News Network tells of a mayor who also acts as a detective. He used an AirTag tracker and a clever ruse to catch a man stealing around thirty historic capstones from an eighteenth-century wall near Rufford. A small-town heritage caper, with a very satisfying ending.

That is all for today, and I hope your Monday has as happy an ending as Luna the budgie's.

Staying with reading, Literary Hub has a lovely account from Santa Cruz, California. On Tuesday the sixth of October, during Banned Books Week, three high school seniors organised a benefit screening of The Librarians, the 2025 documentary. It sold out. I like this story for the quiet fact at its centre: three teenagers, in the middle of a week devoted to arguments about what people may read, decided that the most useful thing they could do was fill a room, raise some money for libraries, and put the case on the screen. It's a small reminder that young people can be among the most committed champions of books, which is something every teacher of literature hopes is true, and sometimes sees confirmed.

From there, I'd like to move to a group of stories about kindness between people, and I think these are the heart of this morning's briefing.

The first comes from Good News Network, and it reads like a short story with a very clean shape. Thirty years ago, a Korean schoolgirl was the victim of a racist attack in which her hanbok, her traditional dress, was slashed. A Japanese teenager placed his coat over her shoulders. She kept that coat for thirty years. And now, at last, it has been returned to the person who gave it to her. Think about what that coat has been all this time: a piece of cloth, certainly, but also a kind of memory held in trust, evidence that on the worst of days somebody chose to step forward rather than look away. There is something almost novelistic about the long wait and the eventual return, the object that carries a whole story and is finally put back into the hands of the one who started it. If you ever wanted a prompt for creative writing with an older class, an object kept for decades and then given back might do very nicely.

Another story of community kindness comes from Upworthy, and it has a sting before the sweetness. An artist had lived in her home for forty years, and when a landlord's family evicted her, the reported reason was to claim the hand-painted murals she had made there. That is a grim start, with art and a lifetime in one place treated as things to be taken. But a neighbour with a paint sprayer offered her a parting gift, and the headline calls it perfect. I'll leave you to discover exactly what the gift was, because the piece itself is worth reading for that moment. What I can say is that it's a story about art and place, and about a neighbour who understood what the place meant to her.

Alongside these, I'd like to recommend something to watch, which suits your taste for strong characters and for documentaries with a humane touch. ARTE Regards has a thirty-two-minute film called Agnes et Amir, living in a shared flat with a centenarian. It dates from 2021, and it's available on ARTE Concert on YouTube until the twenty-eighth of April, twenty thirty, so there's no rush at all. It follows Agnes Jeschke, who is a hundred years old and lives in Berlin, and Amir Farahani, a young Iranian refugee who shares her home. An unlikely friendship across the generations is exactly the sort of thing that can turn into a wonderful character study, and in French, too, if you want to watch it with your more advanced pupils. It would make a gentle Sunday-afternoon watch, perhaps with a cup of something warm, now that the evenings are drawing in above the valley.

Now, a story about a journey, and what a journey. Good News Network reports that Karl Bushby, a British former paratrooper, has finished a walk around the world. He set out from his hometown of Hull in 1998, and twenty-eight years later he has returned to Hull on foot and been reunited with his mother, who was in tears. Twenty-eight years is longer than some of your colleagues have been teaching. I find it hard to picture an undertaking of that length, and I suspect the walking itself was not the only enormous thing about it. But the image the story leaves us with is wonderfully simple: a man coming home, and his mother waiting. It has a perfect arc, in the way the great odyssey stories do, where the destination is not a place on the map so much as a person.

Let me turn now to the animals, since the news provided quite a menagerie this weekend.

Upworthy has a video story about a man who raised an orphaned otter named Leya and then released her back into the wild. He has filmed her swimming out to his kayak, evidently to say hello and to be cuddled. What strikes me is that this is a story about letting go that doesn't end in loss. The otter is free, and she still chooses to come back and see him. It's tender and very visual, and I'd imagine it's even better with the sound on.

From another corner of the animal kingdom, there's the matter of a budgie named Luna in Northampton. Storm Boelo forced open a window, and Luna escaped. She was later found in a storm drain a mile from home, and the reason she was found at all is that a passing driver happened to see her hopping in. A mile is a very long way for a small bird, and a storm drain is about the least likely place to look. Luckily the driver glanced at the right moment, and the story ends well, with Luna safely back where she belongs.

And Upworthy has one more, from Chicago's O'Hare airport. A stranded traveller, delayed there, stepped outside for a cigar. A three-week-old stray kitten bolted out of the bushes and adopted him on the spot. He went back inside with a kitten and, as the headline puts it, a problem. I don't know how the problem was solved, so I'll leave that to the piece itself. But I do enjoy the idea of a long, dull airport delay being rescued by something so small and so decisive.

There's also a more practical animal story, from Good News Network, which is rather encouraging for anyone who cares about the countryside. Scientists in Leipzig have found that volunteer handlers working with their dogs can find invasive plant species in the wild with about seventy-five per cent accuracy. Invasive plants are one of the pressures on biodiversity, and finding them early is a large part of keeping them in check. What I like is how ordinary the method is: people who already love walking with their dogs, putting those remarkable noses to work for the benefit of wild places. It's the sort of research that makes you think of your own walks around Les Adrets and what a good dog might notice that you wouldn't.

On the subject of countryside, I have a little caper for you, again from Good News Network. In England, there is a mayor who also acts as a detective, which is already a very good start for a novel. Someone had been stealing the capstones from an eighteenth-century wall near Rufford, about thirty of them in all, taken across the countryside. The mayor used an AirTag tracker and a clever ruse to catch the man responsible. It has everything: heritage, a modest crime, a bit of gadgetry, and a satisfying ending. If you enjoy a thriller, this is the gentlest possible kind, where the stakes are old stones and the hero is someone in a mayoral chain with a good idea.

Now to language and music, which I know are close to your heart.

Upworthy tells us that Stevie Nicks misunderstood a Southern woman's accent, and that a single vowel inspired one of her best-known songs. It is a brief piece, but I love the idea that a mishearing can become art. It's rather what happens in poetry all the time, where a sound drifts away from its meaning and finds a new one. For a teacher of English, that single vowel is a nice little demonstration of how accent, ear and imagination work together, and it might make a good starting point for a conversation about how songs and poems are born.

And for something purely musical, Upworthy recalls a December nineteen sixty-four performance by The Seekers, described as two minutes of musical perfection. The text is short, and the clip is decades old rather than new, but sometimes a good performance doesn't age at all. If you have two spare minutes with your coffee, it may be a good way to begin the week.

Then a small piece of history, for the pupils who like their facts to arrive with a date. Good News Network notes that on the eighth of November, nineteen sixty-five, the Murder Act received Royal Assent. It abolished the death penalty in the United Kingdom for almost all crimes, with life imprisonment replacing it. The bill was Sydney Silverman's. It's worth remembering how recent that change is: well within living memory, and within the lifetime of many of the authors and playwrights your pupils will meet in the British section. Anyone reading a novel or a play set before that time will be reading about a country where the law was quite different, and that's a useful thing for a student to hold in mind.

Finally, something close to home. The local news site mesinfos reports that free cultural activities for people with disabilities are taking place at the MC2 in Grenoble throughout November. I don't have the individual details of the programme, but the aim is lovely: making sure the theatre and the arts are open to everyone. If you pass the MC2 this month, or know someone who might benefit, it's worth a look at the programme.

So there we are: a coat returned after thirty years, a walker home in Hull, an otter who still swims out to say hello, and three teenagers who filled a room for libraries. I hope one of them keeps you company today, Yamuna.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Monday, the ninth of November.

Let's start close to home, because there's something today. At half past two this afternoon, at the Musée de Grenoble, the Amis du musée are screening Caroline Champetier's twenty twelve film on Berthe Morisot, followed by a talk. It's a chance to see how a filmmaker approaches a painter's life and work. And looking ahead, the museum has another one for your diary: on the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the actor Anne Castillo performs readings from the journal of the sculptor Anne Truitt, directed by Mathieu Barché. An artist's own written voice, in a museum. Rather lovely.

The MC2 has two December dates worth pencilling in. From the second to the fourth, Jean-François Sivadier stages Chekhov's Ivanov, a rare chance to see a major Russian play on stage without leaving the Grenoble basin. And on the third and fourth, there's Mussum, a dance piece by Souhail Marchiche and Mehdi Meghari of Compagnie Dyptik. I've no more detail than that, but contemporary dance, close to home, is reason enough. Also in the local art world, l'Essentiel has a short piece asking what history lies behind the walls of the Magasin-CNAC, one of the city's key contemporary art venues, if you fancy the story of a building you probably know well.

Now, to painting and writing, which seem to be having a good morning. In The Guardian, Cordelia Roche remembers her father, the poet Paul Roche, and his thirty-year passion for the Bloomsbury painter Duncan Grant. Friend and muse, she says, but never lover. It's a personal account tied to a major Grant exhibition, and it's full of the Bloomsbury world of canvas and conversation. The title alone is a stinger: "My father loved Duncan more than he loved us."

Also in The Guardian, a darker tale: the story of Louise Cansot, the model behind "the girl of one hundred portraits." She was murdered in Paris in nineteen forty-nine, and the police forgot her. Her story has inspired two books, a Goncourt-winning novel and a historical research project, which makes it a fine example of fiction and scholarship picking up what the official record dropped.

And from Beaux Arts Magazine, a quick two-minute profile of Séraphine Louis, Séraphine de Senlis, who lived from eighteen sixty-four to nineteen forty-two. A self-taught pioneer of naïve art, with wonderfully exuberant paintings. A vivid life in very few minutes.

On the book pages, Literary Hub has Olivia Laing in conversation about her new novel, The Silver Book. It's set in the world of nineteen seventies Italian cinema, and it's concerned with art, queer love and illusion. The interviewer clearly admires her spellbinding prose, so it may be one to read for the sentences alone. And The Guardian reviews Two Women, Jacqueline Rose's second novel, a fictional biography that alternates between her sister, the philosopher Gillian Rose, and another philosopher, Edith Stein. Biography, memoir and philosophy woven together, and a memorial to Gillian Rose.

A word for the BFI corner, though I should be honest that I only have headlines. There's an article on the sentry's challenge in Hamlet, "Stand and unfold yourself," and what it might say about the royal court. It links directly to a play on the programme for twenty twenty-seven, so it could make a good opening scene for a class. And Vocal has a tribute titled "Celebrating Maya Angelou," whose I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is on the oral themes list. I can't tell you more about its content, but it's there if you want it.

For your evenings, ARTE has a thirty-two-minute documentary from twenty twenty-one, Agnes et Amir, available until April twenty thirty. Agnes Jeschke is a centenarian in Berlin who shares her home with Amir Farahani, a young Iranian refugee. A warm, unlikely friendship between generations, and two strong characters. And if you'd rather have suspense, Collider flags a new Netflix psychological thriller in four parts, which can be watched in under three hours. There's no further detail, but it sounds like a tidy evening binge.

Now some good news, which we always need. The Good News Network tells of a Korean schoolgirl whose hanbok was slashed in a racist attack thirty years ago. A Japanese teenager placed his coat over her shoulders. She kept that coat all this time, and it has now finally been returned to the boy who gave it. A story of kindness and memory with a perfect arc. And from Upworthy, a man who raised an orphaned otter called Leya, then released her, has filmed her swimming out to his kayak for cuddles. The wild, remembering the hand that helped.

Finally, a practical note on school. Students and teachers have called a strike for tomorrow, Tuesday the tenth of November, with demonstrations including a major one expected in Paris. They're pressing the government for more education spending after weeks of school closures and protests. According to franceinfo, the education minister, Edouard Geffray, has again refused to move the baccalauréat dates despite the pupils' protests. Sébastien Lecornu is meeting lycéen and student representatives this afternoon. Worth checking what it means for your timetable tomorrow.
